1.answer: Adding an item: you compute its k positions with the hash functions and set those bits to 1. Looking an item up: you compute the same k positions and check those bits. If any of them is 0 the answer is "no"; if all are 1 the answer is "probably yes".
1.quote: Query** an item: compute its k positions and look at those bits. If any bit is 0, answer "no". If all are 1, answer "probably yes".

2.answer: It can give a false positive: a "probably yes" for an item that was never added, because other items may have already turned on all of that item's bits. It can never give a false negative: adding only ever changes bits from 0 to 1 and nothing resets them, so every item that was added still has all its bits set.
2.quote: Adding an item only changes bits from 0 to 1. Nothing changes a bit back to 0. So every item you added still has all its bits set, and it always gets "probably yes".

3.answer: Other items may share those bits. Clearing them can turn off a bit that another added item needs, so that item then gets a wrong "no". In the example, clearing cat's bit 6 breaks dog.
3.quote: Suppose you remove cat by clearing bits 1 and 6. Dog also uses bit 6. Now a query for dog finds bit 6 at 0 and answers "no", which is wrong.

4.answer: "Probably yes". All of the item's bits are 1, so the filter gives a false positive for every unseen item. This is the extreme end of the over-full case the explanation describes. The explanation does not discuss this case directly; I reasoned it from the query rule.
